byTheNumbers.title: The year in numbers
byTheNumbers.standfirst: Four years of rationing, a wartime labour force with nearly 19.3 million women in it, and the first penicillin on sale to the public.

items.title: Motor vehicles
items.summary: Registrations stood at 31.0 million (25.8 million cars, 5.1 million trucks), only 4.3 million more than in 1930 as new cars were not built for civilians.

sources.label: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Df339-342: Motor vehicle registrations
FHWA Highway Statistics Summary to 1995, Table MV-200: Motor vehicle registrations

items.title: Women in the labour force
items.summary: The female labour force grew from 14.2 million in 1940 to 19.3 million in 1945, 29.2 percent of the total.

sources.label: Wikipedia: American home front during World War II

items.title: Victory gardens
items.summary: By May 1943 there were 18 million victory gardens, 12 million in cities and suburbs and 6 million on farms.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Victory garden

items.title: Wages over the war years
items.summary: Real wages rose 44 percent and average weekly earnings about 70 percent over the four war years.

sources.label: Wikipedia: American home front during World War II

items.metric: Rise in real wages over the war years

sensitivity.note: This item touches on war, famine, epidemic disease or disaster.

items.title: Penicillin output
items.summary: By June 1945 over 646 billion units of penicillin a year were being produced.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Penicillin

byTheNumbers.scarcityNote: Population, life expectancy and household figures for 1945 could not be confirmed from a source we opened.

foodAndKitchen.title: Food and the kitchen
foodAndKitchen.standfirst: Sugar, coffee, meat and butter came by the stamp, and a third of the vegetables eaten came from victory gardens.

items.title: Sugar by the book
items.summary: Sugar sales stopped on 27 April 1942 and restarted on 5 May at half a pound per person per week, about half of normal use, against War Ration Book One, the 'Sugar Book', issued from 4 May.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Rationing in the United States

sensitivity.note: This item touches on war, famine, epidemic disease or disaster.

items.title: Coffee rationed
items.summary: From 29 November 1942 coffee was rationed to one pound every five weeks, about half of normal consumption.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Rationing in the United States

items.title: Red stamps and blue stamps
items.summary: Red stamps rationed meat and butter and blue stamps processed foods; by November 1943 meat, lard, cheese, butter, margarine, canned goods, dried fruit, jams and canned milk were all rationed.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Rationing in the United States

items.title: Grow your own, can your own
items.summary: About one third of the vegetables produced in the United States came from victory gardens, and a poll found 54 percent of Americans gardened for economic reasons and 20 percent out of patriotism.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Victory garden

items.title: Saving cooking fat
items.summary: Families saved used cooking fat to be made into soap, one of the household's contributions to scrap and salvage drives.

sources.label: Wikipedia: American home front during World War II

clothingAndStyle.title: What people wore
clothingAndStyle.standfirst: Fabric rules shortened skirts, nylons vanished and the Victory suit lost its cuffs.

items.title: Order L-85
items.summary: From 8 April 1942 General Limitation Order L-85 limited fabric: wool jackets could be no longer than 25 inches, skirts no longer than 28 inches with 2-inch hems.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1940s in Western fashion

items.title: No stockings, so leg makeup
items.summary: Nylon was short by October 1942 and virtually unobtainable by 1943, so women wore wool, cotton or rayon stockings or painted on leg makeup, drawing seams with eye pencil.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1940s in Western fashion

items.title: The Victory suit
items.summary: Men's Victory suits had no patch pockets, trouser cuffs or pleats, double-breasted suits lost their vests, and jackets had a maximum length.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1940s in Western fashion

items.title: Turbans and snoods in the factory
items.summary: Snoods, turbans and headscarves were popular partly for safety at the factory, where long hair could catch in machinery.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1940s in Western fashion

items.title: Lipstick as morale
items.summary: Lipstick was promoted as a morale builder, in shades such as 'Fighting Red' and 'Jeep Red'.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1940s in Western fashion

items.title: The American Look
items.summary: Dorothy Shaver trademarked 'The American Look' in 1945, and designer Claire McCardell predicted rounder shoulders and fuller skirts to come.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1940s in Western fashion

workAndWages.title: Work and wages
workAndWages.standfirst: More women than ever were in paid work, overtime paid time and a half, and workers were urged to put a tenth of every pay packet into bonds.

items.title: A factory week
items.summary: A manufacturing worker averaged 42.4 hours a week, a railroad worker 46.4 and a coal miner 38.4.

sources.label: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Ba4589-4591: Average weekly hours in manufacturing, 1900-1957

items.title: Women's jobs open and close
items.summary: Manufacturing employed more than 2.5 million additional women by 1944, a 140 percent rise; by 1946 women's employment was about 87 percent of the 1944 level as returning veterans took back jobs.

sources.label: Wikipedia: American home front during World War II

items.title: Overtime and untaxed benefits
items.summary: Overtime paid time and a half, wages were controlled, and employers offered untaxed benefits such as vacation, pensions and health insurance.

sources.label: Wikipedia: American home front during World War II

items.title: The Ten Percent Club
items.summary: Workers were urged to put at least 10 percent of every pay packet into war bonds, which cost three quarters of face value; factories with more than 90 percent taking part flew a 'Minuteman' flag.

sources.label: Wikipedia: American home front during World War II

sensitivity.note: This item touches on war, famine, epidemic disease or disaster.

items.title: Pay before the war
items.summary: In 1941 the median income was $2,000 a year and 8 million workers earned less than the legal minimum.

sources.label: Wikipedia: American home front during World War II

sensitivity.note: This item touches on war, famine, epidemic disease or disaster.

schoolAndChildhood.title: Growing up
schoolAndChildhood.standfirst: Children collected scrap for the war effort.

items.title: Children's scrap drives
items.summary: Children peeled aluminium foil from gum wrappers into balls, collected rubber bands and gathered milkweed, said to be for life jackets.

sources.label: Wikipedia: American home front during World War II

items.title: Care for newborns
items.summary: The EMIC programme gave free maternity and infant care to about 1.2 million wives and children of enlisted men in the four lowest pay grades, and home births fell sharply as more mothers had paid hospital care.

sources.label: Wikipedia: American home front during World War II

schoolAndChildhood.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced school figures for 1945: the NCES table we opened has no entry between 1939-40 and 1949-50.

gettingAround.title: Getting around
gettingAround.standfirst: A thirty-five mile an hour limit and a ration of three gallons a week put the bicycle back on the road.

items.title: A, B and X
items.summary: Gasoline stickers ranked drivers by priority: an A sticker meant 3 to 4 gallons a week, a B up to 8, and an X unlimited.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Rationing in the United States

items.title: Thirty-five miles an hour
items.summary: A national 35 mph limit saved fuel and rubber; a January 1942 Public Roads study found tires lasted four times as long at 35 mph as at 65.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Rationing in the United States
Wikipedia: American home front during World War II

items.title: No new cars
items.summary: Civilian car sales were halted on 1 January 1942 and sightseeing and pleasure driving were banned, so many Americans rode bicycles.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Rationing in the United States
Wikipedia: American home front during World War II

items.title: Deliveries stop
items.summary: Stores that had delivered goods to the door mostly stopped, because of labour shortages and gasoline and tire rationing.

sources.label: Wikipedia: American home front during World War II

healthAndMedicine.title: Health and medicine
healthAndMedicine.standfirst: Penicillin reached ordinary patients in March 1945.

items.title: Penicillin for everyone
items.summary: Penicillin was made available to the general public in the United States on 15 March 1945.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Penicillin

items.title: Millions of doses by 1944
items.summary: Research on fermentation let the United States produce 2.3 million doses of penicillin by spring 1944, and a mouldy cantaloupe from a Peoria market yielded the strain used.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Penicillin

leisureAndFun.title: Evenings, weekends and festivals
leisureAndFun.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced material on films, radio, sport or holidays for 1945.

spotlight.title: Rationing and the home front
spotlight.standfirst: Every man, woman and child had a ration book, and a stamp could buy shoes or sugar, until most rationing ended in August 1945.

items.title: A book for every person
items.summary: Each member of a household, babies included, received a ration book, issued through some 5,500 mostly volunteer local ration boards.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Rationing in the United States

items.title: Stamps and wooden tokens
items.summary: Most stamps did not name the goods or amount, which local newspapers announced; red and blue tokens made of compressed wood fibre were given as change because metal was scarce.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Rationing in the United States

items.title: What took coupons
items.summary: By the end of 1942 coupons covered typewriters, gasoline, bicycles, shoes, rubber footwear, silk, nylon, fuel oil and stoves.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Rationing in the United States

items.title: Doubling up
items.summary: In industrial areas families doubled up in cramped quarters, and the shortage of housing, because non-military building had stopped, lasted until about 1949.

sources.label: Wikipedia: American home front during World War II

items.title: Rationing ends
items.summary: The OPA stopped printing 1946 ration books on 13 August 1945; most rationing ended that August, though sugar continued in some areas into 1946.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Rationing in the United States
